blocks.text: At 3 a.m. a blood culture bottle from a febrile patient flags positive after 14 hours. Within minutes the microbiologist has a Gram stain on the screen, and the ward is phoned with a first answer long before any species name exists. How does a few cells in a bottle become a result, and what do the colours on the slide really tell us?

blocks.markdown: Bacteria reproduce by **binary fission**: one cell grows, replicates its chromosome and divides into two. The time for the population to double under fixed conditions is the **generation time** (doubling time, $g$). It ranges from about 20 minutes for *Escherichia coli* in rich medium to roughly 20 hours for *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, which is why a tuberculosis culture takes weeks.

blocks.title: Exponential growth
blocks.text: If a population starts with $N_0$ cells and doubles every $g$ minutes, then after time $t$ (minutes) there are $N = N_0 \times 2^{t/g}$ cells. This holds only while nutrients are not limiting, that is, during the exponential (log) phase.

blocks.caption: N: cell number at time t; N0: starting number; g: generation time (same units as t)

blocks.markdown: In a closed (batch) culture, growth follows **four phases**. (1) **Lag**: cells adapt, synthesise enzymes and ribosomes, and the number barely rises. (2) **Exponential (log)**: maximal, constant doubling; cells are most uniform and most susceptible to antibiotics that act on growing cells (such as beta-lactams). (3) **Stationary**: nutrients are depleted and waste accumulates, so division balances death and the viable count plateaus; secondary metabolites and toxins are often made. (4) **Death (decline)**: cells die faster than they divide, and some lyse.

blocks.title: Predicting a population
blocks.prompt: A broth is inoculated with 2.0 x 10^3 cells of a bacterium whose generation time is 30 minutes. Assuming no lag and exponential growth throughout, how many cells are present after 3 hours?

steps.text: Convert time to the same unit as g: 3 h = 180 min, so the number of generations is t/g = 180/30 = 6.

blocks.markdown: **Culture media** are designed for a purpose. **Basic (nutrient) media** support many organisms. **Enriched media** contain extra nutrients such as blood or heated blood so that fastidious organisms grow: blood agar for streptococci, and chocolate agar (heated blood) for *Haemophilus* and *Neisseria*. **Selective media** contain agents that inhibit unwanted organisms so the target grows: for example, bile salts and crystal violet inhibit most Gram-positive bacteria. **Differential media** contain an indicator that shows biochemical differences between organisms growing on the same plate: MacConkey agar is both selective (bile salts, crystal violet) and differential, because lactose fermenters make acid and produce pink colonies while non-fermenters stay colourless.

blocks.caption: Types of culture medium
rows: Adds blood or serum for fastidious organisms

blocks.markdown: **The Gram stain** is the first identification step because it takes minutes. The smear is fixed, stained with crystal violet, treated with iodine (forming a crystal violet-iodine complex), decolourised with alcohol or acetone, and counterstained with safranin. **Gram-positive** cells retain the complex and appear **purple**; **Gram-negative** cells lose it and appear **pink**. Reading shape and arrangement adds information: cocci in clusters, cocci in chains, diplococci, bacilli. Combined with the specimen site, the stain narrows the differential and guides early therapy and which medium to inoculate. Some organisms stain poorly or not at all (such as mycobacteria, which need an acid-fast stain, and organisms without a cell wall).

blocks.caption: Gram stain interpretation as a first step

blocks.title: Choosing a plate from a Gram stain
blocks.prompt: A urine smear shows pink bacilli. The lab wants to confirm the organism is a lactose fermenter. Which medium and what result?

steps.text: Pink bacilli are Gram-negative rods, so choose a medium that selects Gram-negative growth: MacConkey agar.
MacConkey also differentiates: lactose fermenters (such as E. coli) acidify the medium and form pink colonies; non-fermenters (such as Pseudomonas) form colourless colonies.

blocks.answer: MacConkey agar; pink colonies indicate lactose fermentation.

items: Lag phase: adaptation, little increase in number.
Exponential phase: constant doubling; most sensitive to growth-dependent antibiotics.
Stationary phase: growth equals death; nutrient limitation.

blocks.title: Culture and stain work together
blocks.text: Gram stain gives a fast, presumptive answer from the specimen directly; culture on appropriate media gives viable growth for identification and susceptibility testing. Neither replaces the other.

blocks.title: Staining and growth pitfalls
blocks.text: Over-decolourisation can make Gram-positive cells look pink, and old cultures may stain variably. A negative Gram stain does not exclude infection. Generation time calculations apply only to the exponential phase.

points: Growth is by binary fission; in the exponential phase N = N0 x 2^(t/g).
The four phases are lag, exponential, stationary and death.
Enriched media add nutrients, selective media inhibit unwanted organisms, differential media reveal biochemical differences.
Gram stain (purple = Gram-positive, pink = Gram-negative) plus shape and arrangement is the first rapid identification step.

questions.stem: In which phase of the batch growth curve do bacteria divide at a constant maximal rate?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: doubling at a constant rate.
distractorRationale.b: Lag phase involves adaptation with little division.
distractorRationale.c: In stationary phase division balances death.
distractorRationale.d: In the death phase more cells die than divide.

questions.explanation: During exponential growth nutrients are plentiful and the number of cells doubles every generation time. Other phases lack either adaptation or nutrient availability.

questions.stem: A laboratory plates a faecal sample onto an agar that contains bile salts and crystal violet and also a lactose-pH indicator. Lactose-fermenting colonies are pink and others are colourless. How is this medium best classified?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bile salts and crystal violet select; the lactose indicator differentiates.
distractorRationale.b: Enrichment adds blood or serum, which is not described.
distractorRationale.c: A basic medium has no inhibitors or indicators.
distractorRationale.d: It also contains an indicator that distinguishes lactose fermenters.

questions.explanation: The inhibitors suppress most Gram-positive organisms, making the plate selective. The pH indicator colours fermenters differently, which is the definition of a differential medium.

questions.stem: A sputum smear from a 58-year-old man shows many purple cocci arranged in chains. Which statement is most justified from the Gram stain alone?

options.text: The organisms are Gram-positive cocci, consistent with streptococci, pending culture
The organism is definitively Staphylococcus aureus

questions.correctOptionText: The organisms are Gram-positive cocci, consistent with streptococci, pending culture

distractorRationale.a: Correct: purple colour indicates Gram-positive; chains suggest streptococci.
distractorRationale.b: Gram-negative bacilli appear pink and rod shaped.
distractorRationale.c: Staphylococci typically appear as clusters, and a stain cannot give a definitive species.
distractorRationale.d: Mycobacteria stain poorly with Gram stain and need an acid-fast stain.

questions.explanation: Gram stain provides a presumptive group by colour, shape and arrangement. Species identification requires culture and further tests.

questions.stem: Which type of culture medium contains extra nutrients such as heated blood to support fastidious organisms?

distractorRationale.b: Selective media inhibit unwanted growth rather than add nutrients.
distractorRationale.d: Transport media preserve organisms and do not support growth.

questions.explanation: Enriched media such as chocolate agar supply factors that fastidious organisms cannot make. They are defined by added nutrients rather than inhibitors or indicators.

questions.stem: A bacterial culture is incubated in a closed flask. After many hours the viable count has plateaued, nutrient levels are low and waste products are accumulating. A beta-lactam is added. Which prediction is best?

options.text: Less killing than in the exponential phase, because beta-lactams act mainly on dividing cells
More killing than in the exponential phase, because stressed cells are less protected
No difference, because beta-lactams act regardless of growth
Complete killing, because stationary cells lack peptidoglycan

questions.correctOptionText: Less killing than in the exponential phase, because beta-lactams act mainly on dividing cells

distractorRationale.b: Stress does not make non-dividing cells more susceptible to wall synthesis inhibitors.
distractorRationale.c: Activity does depend on cell wall synthesis occurring.
distractorRationale.d: Stationary cells still have peptidoglycan; they just make less new wall.

questions.explanation: The plateau means the culture is in stationary phase, where little new peptidoglycan is made. Beta-lactams inhibit cell wall synthesis, so they work best on dividing cells.

questions.stem: A culture grows exponentially from 2.5 x 10^5 cells per mL to 4.0 x 10^6 cells per mL in 100 minutes, with no lag. Calculate the generation time in minutes.
questions.explanation: The fold increase is 4.0 x 10^6 / 2.5 x 10^5 = 16, which is 2^4, so there were 4 generations. The generation time is 100 min / 4 = 25 minutes.

questions.stem: A midstream urine sample is cultured by spreading 0.001 mL (1 microlitre) with a calibrated loop. After incubation 85 colonies are counted. Assuming each colony arose from one viable organism, calculate the bacterial count in the original urine in colony-forming units (CFU) per mL.
questions.explanation: CFU per mL = colonies / volume plated = 85 / 0.001 mL = 85 000. Quantitative culture of this kind distinguishes significant bacteriuria from contamination, although interpretation thresholds vary by guideline.

questions.stem: Sketch and describe the four phases of a bacterial batch growth curve, explaining what is happening to the cells and the nutrient supply in each phase.
markingGuide: Lag: adaptation, enzyme and ribosome synthesis, little increase in number
Exponential: constant maximal doubling, nutrients plentiful, N = N0 x 2^(t/g)
Stationary: nutrient depletion and waste accumulation, division balances death, plateau
Death: viable count falls as cells die and lyse
Clinical or practical link, such as beta-lactam activity depending on growth
questions.explanation: A complete answer names all four phases in order and explains each through cell behaviour and nutrient availability. Linking to a practical consequence shows understanding beyond recall.

questions.stem: Distinguish selective, differential and enriched media. Use MacConkey agar and chocolate agar as examples and explain which Gram stain finding would make each the logical choice.
markingGuide: Selective: inhibitors suppress unwanted organisms (bile salts and crystal violet in MacConkey)
Differential: indicator distinguishes biochemical properties (lactose fermentation gives pink colonies)
Enriched: added blood or heated blood for fastidious organisms (chocolate agar)
MacConkey suited to pink Gram-negative bacilli
Chocolate agar suited to fastidious organisms such as Haemophilus or Neisseria (Gram-negative coccobacilli or diplococci)
questions.explanation: Media are classified by what they add or inhibit, and MacConkey is both selective and differential. The Gram stain narrows the likely group, which guides which medium to inoculate.

questions.stem: Describe the steps of the Gram stain and explain why purple and pink cells result.
markingGuide: Crystal violet applied, then iodine to form a complex
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan retains the complex, so purple
Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan and outer membrane lose the complex, so pink
questions.explanation: The stain is a sequence of dye, mordant, decolouriser and counterstain. The different retention of dye follows wall structure, which is why the result is a first identification step.
